text: Treatment G reduced inflammatory activity and was followed by slower fibrosis progression. The antifibrotic effect was observed equally in patients with and without a measurable inflammatory response, suggesting that inflammation reduction was not necessary for benefit. Nevertheless, because inflammation declined before fibrosis improved, the results prove that Treatment G prevents fibrosis exclusively through suppression of inflammation.

Drug C is believed to improve symptoms through suppression of Biomarker X. Clinical improvement was consistently observed within 24 hours after treatment, whereas Biomarker X did not begin to decline until approximately two weeks later. Despite this temporal sequence, the early clinical response confirms that suppression of Biomarker X is the immediate mechanism responsible for symptom improvement.

Treatment D did not significantly improve overall survival in the full study population. No benefit was detected in the prespecified low-risk or intermediate-risk subgroups. A post hoc analysis suggested improved survival among a small subset of high-risk patients. These findings demonstrate that Treatment D provides a consistent survival benefit across the entire patient population.

Because the study was retrospective and treatment allocation was not randomized, patients receiving Treatment H had less severe disease at baseline. Residual confounding and reverse causation therefore cannot be excluded. After adjustment for measured baseline variables, Treatment H remained associated with lower mortality. These findings establish that Treatment H directly causes a reduction in mortality.

Treatment J was associated with a modest improvement in functional status, although the confidence interval included the possibility of no effect. The analysis was exploratory and was not adjusted for multiple comparisons. The authors therefore concluded that Treatment J definitively produces a large and statistically significant functional benefit.

Treatment K significantly reduced mortality in men, whereas the result was not statistically significant in women. However, the estimated treatment effects were similar in the two groups, and the treatment-by-sex interaction was not statistically significant. The authors therefore concluded that Treatment K is effective only in men and has no benefit in women.

Treatment L was associated with improved quality of life among patients who completed the 12-month follow-up. However, 45% of participants in the Treatment L group discontinued follow-up, mostly because of adverse effects or lack of efficacy, and these patients were excluded from the final analysis. The authors concluded that Treatment L is well tolerated and improves quality of life in nearly all treated patients.

Among patients who survived for at least one year after diagnosis, Treatment M was associated with longer subsequent survival. Patients who died during the first year were excluded because they were not eligible for the landmark analysis. The Treatment M group contained a larger proportion of one-year survivors than the control group, but treatment exposure was assigned using medication use recorded at the one-year landmark. The authors concluded that Treatment M improves survival from the time of diagnosis in all patients.

Treatment N was associated with lower mortality before adjustment. The primary analysis then adjusted for treatment response measured three months after therapy began. Treatment response was strongly affected by Treatment N and was also associated with subsequent mortality. After adjustment for response, the mortality association disappeared. The authors concluded that Treatment N has no survival benefit because the adjusted estimate was null.

The study included only patients admitted to the intensive care unit. Both elevated Biomarker Q and severe underlying disease increased the likelihood of intensive-care admission. Severe underlying disease was also associated with higher mortality. Among intensive-care patients, elevated Biomarker Q was associated with lower mortality. The authors concluded that Biomarker Q protects against death in all patients with the disease.

Treatment O did not meet the prespecified noninferiority margin compared with standard therapy. The confidence interval included differences favoring standard therapy beyond the allowed margin, and the study was not designed as an equivalence trial. Because the primary comparison was not statistically significant, the authors concluded that Treatment O and standard therapy are equally effective.

Treatment P was associated with a lower cumulative incidence of cancer recurrence. However, patients receiving Treatment P had substantially higher early non-cancer mortality, and deaths before recurrence were treated as censoring in the Kaplan–Meier analysis. The cause-specific recurrence hazard was not significantly different between groups. The authors concluded that Treatment P prevents cancer recurrence.

The study evaluated twenty clinical and laboratory outcomes without prespecifying a primary endpoint or adjusting for multiple comparisons. Nineteen outcomes showed no statistically significant difference between Treatment R and control. One exploratory biomarker showed a nominal p value of 0.04, although the finding was not replicated in the validation cohort. The authors concluded that Treatment R has a robust and reproducible therapeutic effect.
